lowering the barrier to build trading bots does not magically give you an edge
there's so much noise right now about how LLMs and agent workflows let anyone build automated trading bots just by typing prompts. but people are seriously confusing "how easy it is to deploy code" with "actually generating alpha".

automating an execution pipeline, fetching news feeds, or setting up basic trailing stops is just a routine engineering task. lately i've been using alphio ai whenever i need to spit out quick research scripts or parse event feeds through natural language, and yeah, it gets a bot running in minutes. but turning an idea into python code doesn't magically validate your underlying trade logic.

most retail bots blow up or bleed money not because the code crashed, but because the market regime shifted, execution friction ate the spread, or the pattern was pure random noise in the first place.

when the mechanical cost of coding a bot drops close to zero, the edge doesn't move into the prompt. the real bottleneck just shifts right back to market microstructure, slippage, and finding actual signal in noisy data.

Asking for out of sample and net of costs is the right filter. One more worth adding: was the test window fixed before running it, or picked after seeing results? “Out of sample” quietly stops being out of sample once you tune the setup a second time.
Getting a bot running in an afternoon is impressive from a software perspective, but it says nothing about whether the underlying strategy has positive expectancy. I'd rather see someone disprove ten bad ideas with clean testing than deploy one beautiful dashboard around an untested signal. We learned this the hard way over the last few months. Generating 100 lines of clean Python with an LLM takes 10 seconds, but prompt generation is maybe 5% of the problem. 



The remaining 95% is the unglamorous, brutal plumbing that AI never warns you about:



1. Broker-side execution quirks: An LLM will happily give you a market order, but pre-market extended hours require strict limit orders with specific routing flags, or the exchange rejects it on the spot.

2. Microstructure traps: During the first 15 minutes of the open, bid-ask spreads can balloon by 30 to 50 bps. Without hard code blocking entry when the Level 2 spread widens, even a theoretical

What was the maximum drawdown during that month?  
What was the largest position size relative to the initial $5k balance?  
Did the bot use martingale sizing after losses, and if so, what was the maximum number of consecutive increases?  
Is the $13k figure closed equity after all trading costs, or does it include floating P&L?

The reason I ask is

That is the right setup. Two places it can still leak:

1. The trial count. DSR is only as honest as N. Variants are correlated, so the raw count overstates the penalty, but the variants the agent dropped mid-run, every parameter tweak, and any change to the universe after seeing results all belong in it. One way to get an effective N: cluster the trials by return correlation and count the clusters (Lopez de Prado's approach).

2. The universe itself. If the agent searches a universe someone chose after looking at the data, that selection happened before the first logged trial, and DSR cannot see it. Freeze the universe and a final holdout period before the agent starts, and look at the hold
